questions.q:
A shop in Jaipur lets Riya try four school bags, each packed with the same books. The shopkeeper notes the total weight of each loaded bag and the area of her shoulders that the two straps press on together.
Bag | Total weight (books + bag) | Area under both straps
P | 60 N | 0.004 m2
Q | 64 N | 0.008 m2
R | 72 N | 0.012 m2
S | 66 N | 0.010 m2
(a) Find the pressure that bag P puts on Riya's shoulders.
(b) Find the pressure for bags Q, R and S.
(c) The shop can stitch wider straps onto bag P. What total strap area would make bag P press on her shoulders with the same pressure as bag R?
(d) Riya walks 2 km to school. Her physiotherapist says the strap pressure must stay below 7000 Pa, and among the bags that meet this, the lighter one is better for a long walk. Her father says she should simply take R because it gives the least pressure. Decide which bag she should take and justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Pressure = Force / Area = 60 N / 0.004 m2 = 15000 Pa. (b) Q: 64 / 0.008 = 8000 Pa; R: 72 / 0.012 = 6000 Pa; S: 66 / 0.010 = 6600 Pa. (c) Bag P would need 60 N / 6000 Pa = 0.01 m2 of strap area. (d) Bag S. Only R (6000 Pa) and S (6600 Pa) are below 7000 Pa; P and Q are not. Of these two, S weighs 66 N against R's 72 N, so S keeps the pressure within the limit and is the lighter load for the 2 km walk. The lowest pressure alone does not decide it once both bags are within the limit.
s: Part (a): 15000 Pa from Force / Area
Part (b): Q 8000 Pa, R 6000 Pa and S 6600 Pa
Part (c): 0.01 m2 found by working back from 6000 Pa
Part (d): S chosen, because R and S both stay below 7000 Pa and S is lighter

questions.q: Kabir pushes a drawing pin into a soft board with a force of 20 N. The flat head touching his thumb has an area of 0.0001 m2; the point touching the board has an area of 0.0000002 m2. How many times greater is the pressure on the board at the point than the pressure on his thumb?
questions.a: 500 times
o: 500 times
1 time, as the force is the same
0.002 times
50 times

questions.q: A 30 N brick rests first on its largest face (area 0.02 m2) and then stands on its smallest face (area 0.005 m2). The pressure it puts on the ground when standing on the smallest face is ___ times the pressure on the largest face.

Read three statements about pressure.
Statement 1: If both the force on a surface and the area it acts on are doubled, the pressure stays the same.
Statement 2: A force of 300 N spread over 0.5 m2 gives a pressure of 150 Pa.
Statement 3: In this chapter, pressure is worked out only for forces that act perpendicular to the surface.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A vegetable seller carrying a heavy basket on her head places a round piece of cloth under it.
Reason (R): The cloth reduces the weight of the basket that acts on her head.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A 200 N crate rests on a floor on a face of area 0.5 m2. Which change will exactly double the pressure it puts on the floor?
questions.a: Turn it onto a face of area 0.25 m2
o: Turn it onto a face of area 0.25 m2
Turn it onto a face of area 1.0 m2
Put a 100 N load on it and keep the same face
Put a 200 N load on it and turn it onto a 1.0 m2 face

questions.q: A 600 N sofa stands on four thin legs that leave dents in a soft carpet. Arun slides one flat wooden board, weighing 40 N, under all four legs. Which statement about the carpet is NOT correct?
questions.a: The force on the carpet becomes smaller
o: The force on the carpet becomes smaller
The force on the carpet rises by 40 N
The pressure on the carpet becomes smaller
The force acts on a larger area of carpet

questions.q: True or False? 'A heavier object always puts a greater pressure on the floor than a lighter object.' Give the verdict, then support it with a pair of objects and numbers of your own.
questions.a: False. Pressure depends on the area as well as the force. For example, a 50 N box resting on 0.01 m2 gives 50 / 0.01 = 5000 Pa, while a much heavier 400 N box resting on 0.2 m2 gives only 400 / 0.2 = 2000 Pa.
s: Verdict: False, because pressure depends on area as well as force
A worked pair where the heavier object gives the lower pressure

questions.q: Four students each wrote down a pair of loads they tested on a sand tray. In which pair do the two loads put the SAME pressure on the sand?
questions.a: 500 N on 2 m2, and 125 N on 0.5 m2
o: 500 N on 2 m2, and 125 N on 0.5 m2
500 N on 2 m2, and 250 N on 0.5 m2
400 N on 4 m2, and 40 N on 0.1 m2
300 N on 3 m2, and 30 N on 0.03 m2

questions.q:
A shopkeeper in Indore lifts a 150 N bucket of water. Its thin wire handle presses on 0.0015 m2 of his palm. He slips a broad plastic sleeve over the handle, so it now presses on 0.006 m2.
(a) Find the pressure on his palm with and without the sleeve.
(b) How many times smaller is the pressure with the sleeve, and why does the bucket now feel easier to carry though it weighs the same?
questions.a: (a) Without the sleeve: 150 / 0.0015 = 100000 Pa. With the sleeve: 150 / 0.006 = 25000 Pa. (b) 4 times smaller. The same weight is spread over a larger area of the palm, so the pressure on the hand is lower.
s: Part (a): 100000 Pa and 25000 Pa
Part (b): 4 times smaller, because the same force is spread over a larger area

questions.q:
A sharp needle and a blunt iron nail are each pushed into a thick cotton cloth with the same force.
(a) Which one goes in more easily, and why?
(b) The force must stay the same. What would have to change about the nail for it to go in as easily as the needle? Say what must happen to the area of its tip.
questions.a: (a) The needle. Its tip has a much smaller area, so the same force gives a much greater pressure on the cloth. (b) The nail's tip must be made smaller (sharpened) until its area is as small as the needle's tip; with the same force on the same small area, the pressure on the cloth becomes the same.
s: Part (a): needle, smaller area gives greater pressure for the same force
Part (b): the nail's tip area must be reduced to that of the needle's tip (sharpen it)

questions.q: Ravi stands on a soft mattress and then lifts one foot. He says: 'My weight has not changed, but the pressure I put on the mattress has now become double.' Is Ravi right? Explain using the idea of pressure, assuming both his feet touch equal areas.
questions.a: Yes, Ravi is right. His weight, the force on the mattress, is the same in both cases. Standing on one foot halves the area that the force acts on. Since Pressure = Force / Area, the same force over half the area gives double the pressure, which is why the foot sinks deeper.
s: Verdict: Ravi is right
The force (his weight) is unchanged while the area is halved
Pressure = Force / Area, so the pressure doubles

questions.q:
The wooden floor of a school stage dents if the pressure on it goes above 200000 Pa. A 1200 N piano stands on three legs.
(a) What is the least total area the three legs must press on so that the floor does not dent?
(b) Each leg actually touches 0.0015 m2 of the floor. Will the floor dent? Show why.
questions.a: (a) Area = Force / Pressure = 1200 / 200000 = 0.006 m2. (b) Yes. The legs touch 3 x 0.0015 = 0.0045 m2, which is less than 0.006 m2, so the pressure is 1200 / 0.0045, about 266667 Pa, more than 200000 Pa.
s: Part (a): 0.006 m2 by working back from the limit
Part (b): yes, 0.0045 m2 gives about 266667 Pa, above 200000 Pa

questions.q: Meera's notebook reads: 'A 240 N suitcase stands on its end, of area 0.04 m2. Pressure = 0.04 / 240 = 0.00017 Pa. If I lay it flat on its side of area 0.12 m2, the pressure will be higher, because more of the suitcase touches the floor.' Find the two mistakes and write the correct values.
questions.a: Mistake 1: she divided area by force. Pressure = Force / Area = 240 / 0.04 = 6000 Pa. Mistake 2: a larger area gives a smaller pressure for the same force, not a higher one. Laid flat, the pressure is 240 / 0.12 = 2000 Pa, which is lower.
s: Formula reversed; correct pressure on its end is 6000 Pa
Larger area lowers pressure, so her reasoning is wrong
Pressure laid flat is 2000 Pa

questions.q:
A bullock cart weighing 3000 N in all keeps sinking into a muddy village road near Wardha. Its four narrow wheels each touch the mud over 0.005 m2. The mud holds a wheel up only while the pressure on it is at most 110000 Pa. The owner can afford one change:
Plan 1: fit four broad wheels, each touching 0.0125 m2, for Rs 6000.
Plan 2: add two more narrow wheels of the same kind, making six, for Rs 3000.
(a) Find the pressure on the mud now.
(b) Find the pressure with Plan 1.
(c) Find the pressure with Plan 2.
(d) He wants the cheaper plan if it keeps the pressure within the limit. Which plan does that rule pick for the empty cart?
(e) At harvest he must carry 1500 N of grain on the cart. With Plan 2 fitted, will the cart stay within the limit? Would Plan 1 have done so? Use this to say which plan is really the better buy.
questions.a: (a) Total area = 4 x 0.005 = 0.02 m2; pressure = 3000 / 0.02 = 150000 Pa. (b) Area = 4 x 0.0125 = 0.05 m2; pressure = 3000 / 0.05 = 60000 Pa. (c) Area = 6 x 0.005 = 0.03 m2; pressure = 3000 / 0.03 = 100000 Pa. (d) Plan 2: 100000 Pa is within 110000 Pa and it costs Rs 3000 less. (e) With Plan 2 the loaded cart gives 4500 / 0.03 = 150000 Pa, above the limit, so it sinks again. With Plan 1 it gives 4500 / 0.05 = 90000 Pa, within the limit. Since he must carry grain, Plan 1 is the better buy in spite of the higher price.
s: Part (a): 150000 Pa from 3000 N over 0.02 m2
Part (b): 60000 Pa
Part (c): 100000 Pa
Part (d): Plan 2, within the limit and cheaper
Part (e): Plan 2 gives 150000 Pa loaded, Plan 1 gives 90000 Pa, so Plan 1 is the better buy

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Bhopal placed the same 25 N brick on smooth, damp sand on each of its three faces and measured how deep a dent it made. Their teacher reminded them that on this sand the depth of the dent is proportional to the pressure (double the pressure, double the depth). Their record:
Face | Area of face | Depth of dent
A | 0.02 m2 | 3 mm
B | 0.01 m2 | 2 mm
C | 0.005 m2 | 12 mm
Conclusion written: 'The brick pushes hardest on face A because it touches the most sand.'
(a) Work out the pressure under each face.
(b) Which row of the record must contain a measuring mistake? Explain.
(c) What is wrong with the group's conclusion?
(d) For a clear print, they need a pressure of at least 4000 Pa on a face of area at least 0.01 m2, and they have only 20 N of extra weights. Which face should they use, and with how much extra weight at least? Justify.
questions.a: (a) A: 25 / 0.02 = 1250 Pa; B: 25 / 0.01 = 2500 Pa; C: 25 / 0.005 = 5000 Pa. (b) Row B. A (1250 Pa, 3 mm) and C (5000 Pa, 12 mm) agree: 4 times the pressure gives 4 times the depth. B has double A's pressure, so its dent should be 6 mm, not 2 mm. (c) The force is the same 25 N on every face; a larger area gives a smaller pressure, so face A presses least hard, not hardest. (d) Face B with at least 15 N extra. Face C gives enough pressure but is smaller than 0.01 m2. Face B needs 4000 x 0.01 = 40 N, so 40 - 25 = 15 N extra, within the 20 N they have. Face A would need 4000 x 0.02 = 80 N, so 55 N extra, more than they have.
s: Part (b): row B; A and C fit depth proportional to pressure, so B should be 6 mm
Part (c): same force, largest area gives the least pressure
Part (d): face B with 15 N extra; C is too small and A needs 55 N

questions.q:
Sana pushes a 200 N box sideways across the floor with a force of 50 N. The box rests on a face of area 0.5 m2.
(a) What pressure does the box put on the floor?
(b) Why is the 50 N push not used in your answer?
questions.a: (a) 200 / 0.5 = 400 Pa. (b) The chapter works out pressure only from forces that act perpendicular to the surface. The weight presses straight down on the floor; the 50 N push acts along the floor, so it is not included.
s: Part (a): 400 Pa from the weight over the area
Part (b): only the perpendicular force is used; the push is along the surface

questions.q: A 200 N school bench rests on four legs with small rubber tips and is leaving dents in a new floor. Three students weighing 400 N each usually sit on it. Which single change lowers the pressure on the floor the most?
questions.a: Fitting each leg with a pad of four times the tip's area
o: Fitting each leg with a pad of four times the tip's area
Adding a fifth leg with the same rubber tip as the others
Letting only two of the three students sit on the bench
Replacing the tips with harder ones of half the area

questions.q: Asha finds that a 60 N tray rests on 10 cm2 of a table and writes the pressure as 6 N/cm2. What is this pressure in pascals? (1 m2 = 10000 cm2)
o: 600 Pa
6 Pa

questions.q: Write a short real-life situation (not a bag, bucket, nail or knife) that is solved by the working 'Pressure = 450 N / 0.15 m2'. Then find the answer and say what it tells us.
questions.a: Example: a 450 N almirah stands on four small feet that together touch 0.15 m2 of the floor; find the pressure on the floor. Pressure = 450 / 0.15 = 3000 Pa, so each square metre of floor under the feet carries a force of 3000 N.
s: A situation where 450 N acts perpendicular on 0.15 m2
Pressure = 3000 Pa
Meaning: 3000 N on each square metre of the surface

questions.q:
Lakshmi carries a 240 N basket of vegetables on her head. Without a pad, the basket's rim presses on 0.0016 m2 of her head. She feels comfortable only if the pressure stays at or below 30000 Pa. She can make one of two cloth pads:
Pad A: weighs 2 N and spreads the load over 0.006 m2.
Pad B: weighs 6 N and spreads the load over 0.012 m2.
(a) Find the pressure on her head with no pad.
(b) What is the least area the load must be spread over for her to be comfortable?
(c) Find the pressure with each pad (count the pad's own weight).
(d) Which pad should she make? Justify.
(e) On market day the basket weighs 330 N. Does the pad you chose still keep her comfortable? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) 240 / 0.0016 = 150000 Pa. (b) 240 / 30000 = 0.008 m2. (c) Pad A: 242 / 0.006 = about 40333 Pa; Pad B: 246 / 0.012 = 20500 Pa. (d) Pad B. Though it is heavier, it spreads the load over a larger area, so the pressure is below 30000 Pa; Pad A's area is smaller than 0.008 m2 and gives more than 30000 Pa. (e) Yes: (330 + 6) / 0.012 = 28000 Pa, still at or below 30000 Pa.
s: Part (a): 150000 Pa
Part (b): 0.008 m2 found by working back from the limit
Part (c): about 40333 Pa for A and 20500 Pa for B
Part (d): Pad B, larger area keeps pressure under the limit despite more weight
Part (e): 28000 Pa, still comfortable

questions.q: A plumber tests a horizontal water pipe by drilling three pinholes at the same point along it: one on top, one on the side and one underneath. All three jets of water come out equally strong. What does this result show?
questions.a: At one point, water presses equally in every direction
o: At one point, water presses equally in every direction
Water presses mainly downward, so the lower jet is fed most
Water presses only along the pipe, in the direction it flows
The air outside pulls water out equally through every hole

questions.q: Three vessels hold water: a narrow glass with 200 mL standing 15 cm deep, a wide bowl with 1500 mL standing 8 cm deep, and a flask with 500 mL standing 12 cm deep. Which order lists the water pressure at their bottoms from greatest to least?
questions.a: Glass, then flask, then bowl
o: Glass, then flask, then bowl
Bowl, then flask, then glass
All three are equal at the bottom
Flask, then glass, then bowl

questions.q:
In a housing society in Pune, the water surface in the rooftop tank is 4 m above the taps of flat 301 and 10 m above the taps of flat 101.
(a) Which flat gets the stronger stream of water, and why?
(b) The society raises the tank by 2 m. Does flat 301 now get as strong a stream as flat 101? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Flat 101. The column of water above its taps is taller (10 m against 4 m), and liquid pressure increases with the height of the column. (b) No. Both streams become stronger, but the columns are now 6 m and 12 m, so flat 101 still has the taller column and the stronger stream.
s: Part (a): flat 101, taller water column means more pressure
Part (b): no, columns become 6 m and 12 m, 101 is still taller

questions.q:
A school in Shimla needs a water tank for its ground-floor drinking taps, which use 4000 L a day. The plumber says the water surface must be at least 5 m above the taps for a usable stream. Two plans:
Plan X: a 2000 L tank on the roof. When full, its water surface is 8 m above the taps.
Plan Y: a wider 5000 L tank on a platform beside the taps. When full, its water surface is 2 m above the taps.
The roof can safely carry at most 3000 kg. Each litre of water has a mass of 1 kg and an empty tank has a mass of 100 kg.
(a) Find the mass a full Plan X tank puts on the roof, and say whether a 5000 L tank could go on the roof instead.
(b) In an activity, two pipes of different widths, filled with water to the same height, made the balloons tied below them bulge equally. The principal says Plan Y must give the stronger stream because it holds more than twice as much water. Use the activity to answer her.
(c) How many times a day must the Plan X tank be filled to meet the school's needs?
(d) Which plan should the school choose? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 2000 kg of water + 100 kg tank = 2100 kg, within the 3000 kg limit. A full 5000 L tank would put 5100 kg on the roof, more than 3000 kg, so it cannot go there. (b) In the activity the pipes held different weights of water, yet the bulges were equal at the same height, so the amount of water does not decide the pressure; the height of the column does. Plan Y's column is only 2 m against Plan X's 8 m, so Plan Y gives the weaker stream. (c) 4000 / 2000 = 2 times a day. (d) Plan X. Plan Y holds more but its 2 m column is below the 5 m the taps need, and a 5000 L tank is too heavy for the roof. Plan X gives an 8 m column within the roof limit; the cost is filling it twice a day.
s: Part (a): 2100 kg, within the limit; a full 5000 L tank (5100 kg) is too heavy
Part (b): equal bulges with unequal amounts show height, not amount, sets the pressure
Part (c): 2 fillings a day
Part (d): Plan X, the only plan above 5 m and within the roof limit, filled twice a day

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: Two pipes of different widths, filled to the same height, make the balloons at their ends bulge equally because they hold equal weights of water.
Statement 2: Water spurting out of holes made at one height all round a bottle shows that water presses on the sides of its container.
Statement 3: The water behind a dam pushes sideways on the wall hardest near the wall's base.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the idea it shows in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. A nurse hangs a saline bottle on a tall stand, well above the patient's arm | a. Liquid pressure does not depend on the amount of liquid
2. Water sprays sideways and upwards from a loose joint in a garden pipe | b. Liquid pressure rises as the liquid column gets taller
3. A narrow jar and a wide jar, filled to the same height, give equal streams from their bottom taps | c. The sideways push of water is greatest near the bottom
4. A dam wall is made much thicker at its base than at its top | d. A liquid presses in all directions

In an activity, two pipes of different widths have identical balloons tied at their lower ends and are filled with water. Tanvi thinks the weight of the water in a pipe decides how much its balloon bulges. Which observation shows that she is wrong?
questions.a: Unequal weights of water at one height gave equal bulges
o: Unequal weights of water at one height gave equal bulges
A balloon bulged more each time more water was poured in
Both balloons bulged as soon as water was poured in
Water spurted from holes made at one height round a bottle

questions.q: True or False? 'Two buckets are filled with water to the same height, but one has a base twice as wide in area as the other. The pressure at their bottoms is the same, yet the wider bucket's bottom is pushed by a larger total force.' Give the verdict, then the reason.
questions.a: True. Pressure at the bottom depends only on the height of the water column, which is the same. Force = Pressure x Area, so the bucket with twice the base area has twice the force on its bottom.
s: Verdict: True
Same height gives the same pressure; force = pressure x area, so the larger base gets the larger force

questions.q:
Anil says two things about water tanks:
(i) 'The deeper a point is below the water surface, the greater the water pressure there.'
(ii) 'So a short, wide tank holding 1000 L with its water 1.2 m deep must have a greater pressure at its bottom than a tall, narrow tank holding 500 L with its water 2.5 m deep.'
Is Anil right, wrong, or partly right? Explain each part.
questions.a: Partly right. (i) is right: a deeper point has a taller column of water above it, so the pressure is greater. (ii) is wrong: pressure depends on the height of the water column, not the amount of water. The tall narrow tank's water is 2.5 m deep against 1.2 m, so its bottom has the greater pressure, even though it holds less water.
s: Verdict: partly right
Part (i) right: taller column above a deeper point
Part (ii) wrong: 2.5 m against 1.2 m, so the narrow tank's bottom has the greater pressure

questions.q: A village builds a small stone wall across a stream to hold water. To save stone, the wall is made equally thick from top to bottom. When the water behind it is deep, where is the wall most likely to crack first, and what design change does the chapter suggest?
questions.a: Near its base. The water pushes sideways on the wall, and this push is largest near the bottom where the water is deepest. The wall should be built much broader at the base than at the top, as dams are.
s: Near the base, where the sideways water pressure is largest
Make the base broader than the top

questions.q:
A steel jug, a bucket and a washing tub are each filled with water to a depth of 24 cm. The water pressure at the bottom of the jug is about 2400 Pa. Their base areas are: jug 0.01 m2, bucket 0.03 m2, tub 0.08 m2.
(a) What is the water pressure at the bottom of the bucket and of the tub? Give the reason.
(b) Find the force of the water on the base of each container.
(c) The force on the bucket's base is three times that on the jug's base, yet the pressures are equal. Explain how both can be true.
(d) Some water is now poured out of the tub until it is only 10 cm deep. Is the pressure at the tub's bottom now greater or less than at the jug's bottom? Why?
questions.a: (a) About 2400 Pa in both, because the water stands at the same height (24 cm) and pressure depends only on the height of the column, not the shape or size of the vessel. (b) Force = Pressure x Area: jug 2400 x 0.01 = 24 N; bucket 2400 x 0.03 = 72 N; tub 2400 x 0.08 = 192 N. (c) Pressure is the force on each unit of area. The bucket's base has three times the area, so the same pressure acting on it adds up to three times the force. (d) Less, because the column of water above the tub's bottom (10 cm) is now shorter than the jug's (24 cm).
s: Part (a): 2400 Pa in both, same height of column
Part (b): 24 N, 72 N and 192 N from force = pressure x area
Part (c): equal pressure over three times the area gives three times the force
Part (d): less, shorter column

questions.q:
Rani's balloon is tied below pipe A, which holds water to a height of 30 cm.
(a) She pours out half the water. What happens to the bulge, and why?
(b) She pours this half into pipe B, whose cross-section has half the area of pipe A's, with an identical balloon tied below. Compare B's bulge with A's bulge at the start.
questions.a: (a) The bulge becomes smaller, because the water column is now only 15 cm tall and pressure depends on its height. (b) The same. Half the water in a pipe of half the cross-section stands 30 cm tall again, so the pressure, and the bulge, equal what A had at the start.
s: Part (a): smaller bulge, column falls to 15 cm
Part (b): same bulge, the column in B is 30 cm tall

questions.q: In the bottle activity, four holes are made near the bottom of a plastic bottle, all at the same height, and water spurts out equally from all of them. Explain (i) what this shows about the direction in which water presses, and (ii) why the holes must be at the same height for this conclusion to be fair.
questions.a: (i) Water comes out through the sides in every direction, so water presses on the sides of the container, not just the bottom; liquids press in all directions. (ii) Pressure depends on the height of the water column above a hole. If the holes were at different heights, the streams would differ because of their depth, and we could not tell whether direction mattered. Same height keeps depth equal, so equal streams show the push is the same in every direction.
s: Water presses sideways, in all directions
Pressure depends on the height of water above each hole
Same height keeps depth equal, so only direction is being compared

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The water pressure at the bottom of a full 50 L drum is greater than at the bottom of a full 1 L bottle of the same height.
Reason (R): The pressure exerted by a liquid depends on the height of its column, not on the amount of liquid.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Lucknow used a tall glass tank with small windows covered by identical thin rubber sheets. They filled it with water and measured how far each sheet bulged out. Windows 1, 2 and 4 were read twice and gave the same values both times; window 3 was read only once. Their record:
Window | Wall | Depth below water surface | Bulge
1 | front | 10 cm | 2 mm
2 | front | 20 cm | 4 mm
3 | front | 30 cm | 3 mm
4 | back | 20 cm | 4 mm
(a) One reading does not fit the others. Which one, and why?
(b) What do windows 2 and 4, taken together, show?
(c) An aquarium maker uses this result. Which strip of the glass wall of a fish tank must be the strongest? Give the reason.
(d) She has cheap thin glass that is safe only where the water is at most 50 cm deep; deeper parts need costly thick glass. She can build either Tank P, 60 cm deep, or Tank Q, wider and 45 cm deep, holding the same amount of water. Which tank lets her use only thin glass? Justify, and say what the other tank would need.
questions.a: (a) Window 3. It is the deepest, so the water pressure there is the greatest; its bulge should be more than the 4 mm at 20 cm, not 3 mm. (b) At the same depth, the bulge is the same on the front and back walls, so water presses sideways equally in different directions at one level. (c) The bottom strip, because the sideways pressure of the water is greatest near the bottom, where the column above is tallest. (d) Tank Q. Pressure depends on the depth of the water, not the amount, and Q's water is only 45 cm deep, within the 50 cm limit, so thin glass is safe everywhere. Tank P is 60 cm deep, so the strip below 50 cm (its bottom 10 cm) would need thick glass.
s: Part (a): window 3, the deepest window should bulge most
Part (b): equal bulge at equal depth on opposite walls, so equal sideways pressure
Part (c): the bottom strip, greatest pressure near the bottom
Part (d): Tank Q, 45 cm is within the limit; P needs thick glass in its bottom 10 cm

questions.q:
A plastic bottle has two holes, each covered by a stretched piece of balloon rubber: one in its base and one in its side, 6 cm above the base. Water is poured in until it stands 20 cm deep.
(a) Will the rubber on the side hole bulge as well as the one on the base? Why?
(b) Which rubber bulges more? Give the reason with numbers.
questions.a: (a) Yes. A liquid presses in all directions, on the sides of a container as well as on its bottom, so the side rubber is pushed out too. (b) The base rubber. It is 20 cm below the water surface, while the side hole is only 20 - 6 = 14 cm below it, and the pressure increases with the height of the water column above.
s: Part (a): yes, a liquid presses on the sides as well as the bottom
Part (b): the base rubber, 20 cm of water above it against 14 cm

questions.q: The water pressure at the bottom of a washing tub is 1500 Pa and its base has an area of 0.08 m2. The water pushes down on the base with a total force of ___ N.

An engineer planning a dam on a river says: 'The wall must be much broader at the bottom than at the top. But the wall need not be made broader just because the lake behind it will stretch back for 20 km instead of 5 km.' Justify both parts of her statement, and say what change to the lake WOULD need a stronger wall.
questions.a: (1) Water stored behind a dam presses horizontally on the wall (and vertically on the floor). (2) This sideways pressure is largest near the bottom, where the column of water above is tallest. (3) So a broad base is needed to withstand it, and it also supports the structure of the dam. (4) The length of the lake only changes the amount of water. Liquid pressure depends on the height of the column, not the amount (pipes of different widths filled to the same level give equal bulges), so a longer lake of the same depth does not raise the pressure on the wall. (5) Raising the water level, making the lake deeper at the wall, would increase the pressure and need a stronger wall.
s: Water presses horizontally on the dam wall
The sideways pressure is largest near the bottom
A broad base withstands it and supports the structure
A longer lake adds amount, not height, so pressure is unchanged
A higher water level would need a stronger wall

questions.q: Javed takes the cap off a full water bottle and makes one hole near the bottom and another near the top, on the same side. What will he see?
questions.a: A stronger stream from the lower hole
o: A stronger stream from the lower hole
Equal streams, as water presses equally in all directions
A stronger stream from the upper hole, nearer the open top
Water from the lower hole only, as water presses downward

questions.q: A shopkeeper claims that his new water jar, which widens towards the top, gives a stronger stream from its bottom tap than an ordinary straight jar, 'because the wide top holds extra water that presses down'. Both jars are filled to the same height. Show that his claim cannot be true.
questions.a: The pressure at the tap depends only on the height of the water column above it. Both jars are filled to the same height, so the pressure at their bottom taps is equal. The extra water in the wide top does not raise the pressure, just as the wider pipe in the balloon activity, holding more water, gave the same bulge. So the streams are equally strong.
s: Pressure at the tap depends only on the height of the column
Same height, so equal pressure at both taps
Extra amount of water does not add pressure, so the streams are equal

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the paper-plate activity, the plate is harder to lift when the chart sheet covering it is folded than when the same sheet is spread out.
Reason (R): Air presses only downward on a sheet, so a folded sheet, being thicker, receives a larger push.
questions.a: A is false, and R is also false
o: A is false, and R is also false
A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.q: An empty steel tiffin box with a tight lid sits on a table. The lid has an area of 0.02 m2, so the outside air pushes down on it with about 2000 N, yet the lid does not cave in. Why?
questions.a: The air sealed inside presses out equally on the lid
o: The air sealed inside presses out equally on the lid
Air presses only on the table, so the lid feels no push
Steel is too heavy for a push of the air to move it
Air presses only on soft things such as skin and rubber

questions.q: A barometer at Shillong reads 100800 Pa at 9 a.m. By noon the air pressure has dropped by 6 hPa. The noon reading, written in millibars, is ___ mb.

(a) Use this to estimate the atmospheric pressure in pascals.
(b) Write the same pressure in millibars.
s: Part (a): 0.0225 m2 and about 100000 Pa
Part (b): 1000 mb using 1 mb = 100 Pa

Statements 1 and 2 only

questions.a: The air inside presses on every part of the balloon's wall
o: The air inside presses on every part of the balloon's wall
The air outside squeezes the balloon into a fatter shape
The air from his mouth moves only forward, so it bunches up
The rubber pulls itself outward once it gets a little air

questions.q: True or False? 'We are not crushed by the atmosphere because air is so light that its pressure on us is tiny.' Give the verdict, then the correct explanation.
questions.a: False. Atmospheric pressure is large: the air pushes on a 15 cm x 15 cm patch with nearly 2250 N, about the force of gravity on a 225 kg mass. We are not crushed because the pressure inside our bodies, caused by the movement of fluids and gases in our tissues and organs, is equal to the atmospheric pressure and balances it.
s: Verdict: False; atmospheric pressure is large (about 2250 N on 15 cm x 15 cm)
The pressure inside the body equals it and balances it

questions.q: Diya holds her closed notebook up in the air. Its cover has an area of 0.06 m2. Taking atmospheric pressure as 100000 Pa, show that the air cannot be pressing on this cover with just a few newtons. Then explain why Diya still lifts the notebook easily.
questions.a: Force = Pressure x Area = 100000 x 0.06 = 6000 N, which is thousands of newtons, not a few. She can still lift it easily because air presses in all directions: air also presses up on the notebook from below with nearly the same pressure, so the pushes from above and below balance.
s: So the force on the cover is thousands of newtons, not a few
Air also pushes from below, so the forces balance

questions.q: In the paper-plate activity, lifting the plate is harder when it is covered by the unfolded chart sheet than by the same sheet folded. Ajay explains: 'A sheet becomes heavier when it is spread out, so the plate is harder to lift.' Is Ajay right? Give the chapter's explanation.
questions.a: No. The sheet's weight does not change when it is unfolded. Unfolding increases the area of the sheet. Air presses on the sheet, and the same air pressure acting on a larger area gives a larger total force, so more effort is needed. This shows that air exerts pressure.
s: Verdict: Ajay is wrong; the weight is unchanged
Unfolding increases the area the air presses on
Same pressure on a larger area gives a larger force, so lifting is harder

questions.q: The atmosphere pushes on a 15 cm x 15 cm patch with nearly 2250 N. About how large is its push on a window pane of 30 cm x 30 cm?

At the same moment, the weather station at Sagar reports 1006 mb and the one at Damoh reports 100400 Pa.
(a) Which town has the higher air pressure?
(b) By how many hectopascals is it higher?
questions.a: (a) Sagar: 1006 mb = 1006 x 100 = 100600 Pa, which is more than 100400 Pa. (b) 100600 - 100400 = 200 Pa, and 1 hPa = 100 Pa, so 2 hPa.
s: Part (a): Sagar, after converting 1006 mb to 100600 Pa
Part (b): 200 Pa = 2 hPa

questions.q:
Ishaan wants to hang a 100 N lamp from a rubber sucker stuck to the underside of a glass shelf, so the lamp pulls straight down, at right angles to the glass. The shelf is narrow: a cup larger than 0.0035 m2 will not fit on it. For safety, the sucker must hold at least 125 N, a quarter more than the lamp's weight. A shop tests three suckers. The air pressure outside is 100000 Pa.
Sucker | Area of cup | Pressure left inside the cup after pressing
S1 | 0.002 m2 | 40000 Pa
S2 | 0.004 m2 | 80000 Pa
S3 | 0.003 m2 | 50000 Pa
(a) Explain why a pressed sucker stays stuck to the glass.
(b) What pull would be needed to pull S1 off the glass?
(c) Find the pull needed for S2 and S3. S2 has the biggest cup; why is it not the hardest to pull off?
(d) Which sucker should Ishaan use? Justify using both conditions.
questions.a: (a) Pressing pushes most of the air out of the cup, so the pressure inside is lower than the air pressure outside; the higher outside pressure holds the sucker against the glass. (b) A pull must overcome the pressure difference over the cup's area: (100000 - 40000) x 0.002 = 120 N. (c) S2: (100000 - 80000) x 0.004 = 80 N; S3: (100000 - 50000) x 0.003 = 150 N. S2 kept much of its air, so the pressure difference across it is small, and even its large area gives only 80 N. (d) S3. S2 is too big for the shelf and holds only 80 N. S1 fits but holds 120 N, less than the 125 N needed. S3 fits (0.003 m2) and holds 150 N, more than 125 N.
s: Part (a): reduced pressure inside, higher outside pressure holds it
Part (b): 120 N from pressure difference x area
Part (c): 80 N and 150 N; S2's small pressure difference outweighs its big area
Part (d): S3, the only sucker that fits and holds at least 125 N

questions.q:
In the paper-plate activity, a chart sheet folded twice covers only a quarter of the area it covers when unfolded.
(a) How many times larger is the force of the air on the unfolded sheet than on the folded one?
(b) Why do both sheets have to weigh the same for this activity to show that air exerts pressure?
questions.a: (a) 4 times, since the same air pressure acts on 4 times the area. (b) If the weights differed, the extra effort could be due to the heavier sheet. With equal weights, the only change is the area, so the extra effort must come from the air pressing on a larger area.
s: Part (a): 4 times, same pressure on 4 times the area
Part (b): equal weight leaves area as the only change, so the extra effort is due to air

questions.q:
A teacher pumps most of the air out of a closed, empty square oil tin, and the tin's sides are seen to cave inwards. Each side of the tin is 0.2 m x 0.2 m. Take the air pressure outside as 100000 Pa; after pumping, the pressure inside is 30000 Pa.
(a) Find the force of the outside air on one side.
(b) Find the force of the air left inside on the same side.
(c) Find the net force on that side and its direction.
(d) Before pumping, the same outside air pressed on the tin, but it did not cave in. Why?
(e) The teacher now opens a small cap on the tin and air rushes in. What happens to the net force on that side, and why?
questions.a: (a) Area = 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.04 m2; force = 100000 x 0.04 = 4000 N. (b) 30000 x 0.04 = 1200 N. (c) 4000 - 1200 = 2800 N, pushing inward, so the side caves in. (d) Before pumping, the air inside was at the same pressure as outside and pushed outward equally, balancing the outside push (just as the pressure inside our bodies balances the atmosphere). (e) Air rushes in from the higher pressure outside to the lower pressure inside until the pressure inside again equals 100000 Pa. The inward and outward forces on the side then balance, so the net force becomes zero.
s: Part (a): 4000 N
Part (b): 1200 N
Part (c): 2800 N inward
Part (d): equal pressure inside and outside balanced each other
Part (e): air flows in until the pressures are equal, so the net force becomes zero

questions.q:
The weather club of a Mysuru school wrote one air-pressure reading each morning on its notice board, but different members used different units.
Day | Reading as written
Monday | 1009 mb
Tuesday | 100700 Pa
Wednesday | 1012 hPa
Thursday | 1004 Pa
(a) Write the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday readings in hPa and say which of the three days had the highest pressure.
(b) Use the chapter's figure (nearly 2250 N on a 15 cm x 15 cm patch) to show that Thursday's '1004 Pa' cannot be the air pressure, and suggest what was meant.
(c) One member says Monday's and Wednesday's readings cannot be compared at all, because one is in millibars and the other in hectopascals. Judge this, and give the difference between the two days in pascals.
questions.a: (a) Monday 1009 hPa (1 mb = 1 hPa, both 100 Pa); Tuesday 100700 / 100 = 1007 hPa; Wednesday 1012 hPa. Wednesday was highest. (b) At 1004 Pa, the force on a 0.0225 m2 patch would be only 1004 x 0.0225, about 22.6 N, far below the nearly 2250 N the chapter gives (which means about 100000 Pa). So the reading must have been 1004 hPa (or 1004 mb). (c) The member is wrong: 1 mb and 1 hPa are both 100 Pa, so the numbers compare directly. Wednesday was higher by 1012 - 1009 = 3 hPa = 300 Pa.
s: Part (a): 1009, 1007 and 1012 hPa; Wednesday highest
Part (b): about 22.6 N against nearly 2250 N, so it was 1004 hPa or mb
Part (c): wrong, mb and hPa are both 100 Pa; difference 300 Pa

questions.q:
A newspaper science column says: 'The air above a 2 m x 1.5 m bed pushes down on it with a force equal to the weight of a 30000 kg truck.' The chapter says the air pushes on a 15 cm x 15 cm patch with about 2250 N, the force of gravity on a 225 kg mass. Take the air pressure as 100000 Pa.
(a) Find the force of the air on the top of the bed.
(b) Use the chapter's figures to find the force of gravity on 1 kg, and so on the 30000 kg truck.
(c) Is the column's claim right? Give your verdict.
(d) Why is the bed not crushed by this force?
(e) On a stormy day the pressure is 990 hPa. Find the force on the bed then, and say whether the column's comparison is still fair.
questions.a: (a) Area = 2 x 1.5 = 3 m2; force = 100000 x 3 = 300000 N. (b) 2250 N / 225 kg = 10 N for each kg, so the truck's weight is 30000 x 10 = 300000 N. (c) Yes, the claim is right: both are 300000 N. (d) Air presses in all directions: the air under and around the bed pushes up and sideways with nearly the same pressure, so the pushes balance. (e) 990 hPa = 99000 Pa; force = 99000 x 3 = 297000 N. This is only 3000 N (1 percent) less, so the comparison is still fair.
s: Part (a): 300000 N on 3 m2
Part (b): 10 N per kg, truck 300000 N
Part (c): verdict, the claim is right
Part (d): air pushes from below and the sides too, so the forces balance
Part (e): 297000 N, about 1 percent less, still fair

questions.q:
Two identical rubber suckers are pressed firmly, one onto a glass window and one onto a rough cement wall. The one on the glass stays; the one on the cement falls off at once.
(a) Explain why the sucker on the cement wall does not stay.
(b) Would a sucker with a much bigger cup stay on the cement wall? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) On the rough wall, air leaks in through the gaps under the rim, so the pressure inside the cup soon equals the air pressure outside. With no pressure difference, nothing holds the sucker against the wall. (b) No. The holding force comes from the pressure difference acting on the cup's area; if air leaks in, the difference is zero, and zero difference on any area gives no holding force.
s: Part (a): air leaks in, so no pressure difference holds it
Part (b): no, a bigger area with zero pressure difference still gives no force

questions.q: A rubber sucker holding a soap dish on a bathroom tile falls off after a few hours. Rohan notices that a little air has slowly seeped in under its rim. Explain, in three linked steps using pressure, why the sucker fell.
questions.a: (1) When pressed, most air was pushed out of the cup, so the pressure inside was lower than the air pressure outside, and this difference held it on. (2) As air seeped in, the pressure inside the cup rose towards the outside pressure. (3) The pressure difference became too small to hold the sucker and the dish, so the outside air no longer held it against the tile and it fell.
s: At first, low pressure inside and higher outside held it on
Air seeping in raised the inside pressure
The pressure difference became too small to hold it, so it fell

questions.q:
On a sunny afternoon, three readings of air pressure were taken near a fishing village on the Odisha coast.
Place | Air pressure at 2 p.m.
A boat 3 km out at sea | 1012 hPa
The beach | 1010 hPa
A farm 2 km inland | 1007 hPa
(a) In which direction does the wind blow between the boat and the beach? Give the rule you used.
(b) Is this a sea breeze or a land breeze? Explain why the pressure is lowest over the land at this time.
(c) Predict how the pattern of pressure over the land and the sea changes at night, and the wind direction that results.
(d) Raju's small boat has only a sail, and he wants the wind behind him both on the way out to the fishing ground and on the way back. Plan 1: leave at 2 p.m. and return at 11 p.m. (9 hours at sea). Plan 2: leave at 10 p.m. and return at 1 p.m. the next day (15 hours at sea). Which plan should he choose? Justify.
questions.a: (a) From the boat towards the beach (sea to land), because air moves from a region of higher pressure (1012 hPa) to lower pressure (1010 hPa). (b) A sea breeze. During the day the land heats up faster than the water, so the air above the land becomes warmer and lighter and rises, leaving low pressure over the land. (c) At night the water is warmer than the land, so the low pressure forms over the sea instead; the wind then blows from the land to the sea (land breeze). (d) Plan 2, though it keeps him at sea longer. At 10 p.m. the land breeze blows from land to sea and carries him out; at 1 p.m. the sea breeze blows from sea to land and brings him back. Plan 1 has the wind against him both ways: the 2 p.m. sea breeze blows towards the shore and the 11 p.m. land breeze blows out to sea.
s: Part (a): sea to land, from higher to lower pressure
Part (b): sea breeze; land heats faster, warm air rises, low pressure over land
Part (c): at night low pressure over the warmer sea, wind from land to sea
Part (d): Plan 2, land breeze takes him out at night and sea breeze brings him back by day

questions.q: Two nearby weather stations read 1008 hPa and 1006 hPa on Monday, and 1011 hPa and 1003 hPa at the same time on Tuesday. On which day is the wind between them stronger, and why?
questions.a: Tuesday, as the pressure difference is four times larger
o: Tuesday, as the pressure difference is four times larger
Neither, as the average of the two is 1007 hPa both days
Tuesday, as one station there reads the highest pressure
Monday, as both of its readings are closer to 1007 hPa

True or False? 'If you blow harder into the gap between two hanging balloons, they come together faster, even though you are blowing air into the space between them.' Give the verdict, then the reason.
questions.a: True. Fast-moving air between the balloons is at a lower pressure than the still air around them, so the higher pressure outside pushes them inward. Blowing harder makes the air faster and the pressure between them lower, so they are pushed together faster.
s: Verdict: True
Faster air between them means lower pressure, so the outside air pushes them in faster
