A weather club on a Chennai beach recorded these temperatures one day.
Time | Land | Sea
2 a.m. | 23 C | 27 C
7 a.m. | 25 C | 26 C
3 p.m. | 36 C | 29 C
10 p.m. | 26 C | 28 C
At which of these times was the breeze blowing from the sea to the land?
questions.a: At 3 p.m., when the land was the warmer
o: At 3 p.m., when the land was the warmer
At 2 a.m., when the sea was warmest of all
At 10 p.m., when the sea was the warmer
At 7 a.m., when the sea was slightly warmer

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When an inflated balloon is joined by a straw to an empty one, the air stops flowing before the inflated balloon is empty.
Reason (R): Air moves only from a region of higher air pressure to a region of lower air pressure.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
The air pressure inside cycle tube A is 250000 Pa and inside tube B is 180000 Pa. The air outside is at 100000 Pa. Both get punctured at the same moment.
(a) From which tube does the air rush out faster at first? Explain.
(b) When does the air stop coming out of a punctured tube?
questions.a: (a) Tube A. The pressure difference between inside and outside is 150000 Pa for A but only 80000 Pa for B, and air escapes faster when the pressure difference is larger. (b) When the pressure inside the tube becomes equal to the air pressure outside, as air flows only from higher to lower pressure.
s: Part (a): tube A, larger pressure difference (150000 Pa against 80000 Pa)
Part (b): when inside and outside pressures become equal

questions.q: Sunita says: 'At night the land breeze blows from the land to the sea because the land is then warmer than the sea, so its warm air pushes out over the water.' Is she right? Explain what really happens at night.
questions.a: No, she is wrong. At night the water is warmer than the land, not the other way round. The warm air over the sea rises, so a low-pressure area forms over the sea. Air then moves from the higher pressure over the cooler land to the lower pressure over the sea, giving the land breeze. Warm air rises; it does not push sideways out over the water.
s: Verdict: Sunita is wrong
At night the sea is warmer, so low pressure forms over the sea
Air moves from higher pressure over the land to lower pressure over the sea

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the idea that explains it in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Two hanging balloons swing together when air is blown between them | a. The land is warmer, so low pressure forms over it
2. Air hisses out of a punctured cycle tube until it goes flat | b. Letting wind pass through reduces the force on a surface
3. A banner with holes cut in it survives a storm that tears a solid one | c. Air flows from high to low pressure until the pressures are equal
4. A beach flag points inland on a sunny afternoon | d. Fast-moving air is at a lower pressure
Passengers are asked to stand behind a yellow line on a railway platform when a fast train passes without stopping. Which reason fits the chapter's ideas?
questions.a: Fast air by the train is at low pressure, so still air pushes people in
o: Fast air by the train is at low pressure, so still air pushes people in
The fast-moving air beside the train pushes people back off the platform
The heavy train pulls the air and the people towards itself by its weight
Air beside a fast train is at high pressure and pushes people towards it

questions.q:
Two empty, light plastic bottles lie on their sides on a smooth table, 5 cm apart and parallel.
(a) Rahul blows hard through the gap between them. Predict how the bottles move, and why.
(b) He now blows hard along the outer side of just one bottle instead. Which way does that bottle roll? Explain.
questions.a: (a) They roll towards each other. The fast-moving air in the gap is at a lower pressure, so the higher pressure of the still air on their outer sides pushes them together. (b) It rolls outward, away from the other bottle, towards the fast air. Now the low pressure is on its outer side, and the still air in the gap, at higher pressure, pushes it outward.
s: Part (a): together, low pressure in the fast-moving gap
Part (b): outward, because the low pressure is now on its outer side

questions.q:
During a storm in coastal Andhra Pradesh, high-speed winds blow over a house with all its doors and windows shut. The pressure of the air inside the house is 100000 Pa, but just above its 40 m2 roof it falls to 99000 Pa. The loosely fixed roof sheets weigh 15000 N in all.
(a) Why is the pressure above the roof lower than inside the house?
(b) Find the upward force on the roof due to the pressure difference.
(c) Will the roof stay in place? Compare with its weight.
(d) The family opens doors and windows on both sides of the house, and the pressure difference falls to 200 Pa. Find the upward force now and say whether the roof stays.
(e) Explain why opening the doors and windows reduced the pressure difference.
questions.a: (a) High-speed winds are accompanied by reduced air pressure, so the fast wind over the roof creates a low-pressure area above it. (b) Pressure difference = 100000 - 99000 = 1000 Pa; force = 1000 x 40 = 40000 N upward. (c) No. 40000 N upward is more than the 15000 N weight of the loosely fixed roof, so it may be lifted off. (d) 200 x 40 = 8000 N, which is less than 15000 N, so the roof stays. (e) With the doors and windows open, the same wind also moves through the house, lowering the pressure inside too, so the difference between inside and above the roof becomes much smaller.
s: Part (a): fast wind brings lower pressure above the roof
Part (c): 40000 N exceeds 15000 N, roof may lift
Part (d): 8000 N, less than the weight, roof stays
Part (e): wind through the house lowers the inside pressure too, so the difference shrinks

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Ranchi hung two equal balloons 8 cm apart from a stick and blew air into the gap through a straw. Their record:
Trial | How they blew | What the balloons did | Time to touch
T1 | gently | moved towards each other | 3 s
T2 | hard | moved towards each other | 1 s
T3 | hard | moved apart | -
T4 | did not blow | stayed still | -
(a) Which trial does not fit the others, and why does the chapter say it cannot be right?
(b) What do trials T1 and T2, taken together, show?
(c) Why did the group include trial T4?
(d) Two light cloth tents, with their flaps closed, are pitched close together in an open field, and a strong wind blows through the narrow gap between them. Predict whether their facing walls will bulge towards or away from each other, and justify.
questions.a: (a) T3. Blowing between the balloons makes the air in the gap move fast, which lowers the pressure there, so the higher pressure outside pushes them together, never apart. (b) Blowing harder made them meet faster (1 s against 3 s): faster air gives a lower pressure between them, so they are pushed in more strongly. (c) To show that, without blowing, the balloons do not move, so the movement in T1 and T2 is caused by the moving air. (d) Towards each other. The fast wind in the gap lowers the pressure there, while the still air inside each closed tent is at higher pressure, so it pushes each facing wall outward into the gap, and the two walls bulge towards each other.
s: Part (a): T3; fast air lowers pressure, so they cannot move apart
Part (b): faster air, lower pressure, they meet faster
Part (c): T4 shows no movement without moving air
Part (d): towards each other, the higher pressure inside each tent pushes its wall into the low-pressure gap

questions.q:
A weather officer in Nagpur records the air pressure at a central station C and at four stations around it, each 20 km from C, at the same moment.
Station | Pressure
C | 1003 hPa
N | 1010 hPa
E | 1004 hPa
S | 1012 hPa
W | 1007 hPa
(a) In which direction does the wind blow between each outer station and C? Give the rule.
(b) Between which station and C is the wind fastest? Give the pressure difference in pascals.
(c) Between which station and C is the wind gentlest, and why?
(d) An hour later C reads 1007 hPa while the others are unchanged. What happens to the wind between W and C, and between E and C?
(e) Explain why the wind into C cannot go on for long unless something keeps C's pressure low, and say what the chapter says can do that.
questions.a: (a) From every outer station towards C, because air moves from higher pressure to lower pressure and C has the lowest pressure (1003 hPa). (b) Between S and C: 1012 - 1003 = 9 hPa = 900 Pa, the largest difference, and the speed of air is higher when the pressure difference is higher. (c) Between E and C: the difference is only 1 hPa (100 Pa), the smallest. (d) W and C are now both 1007 hPa, so the wind between them stops. E (1004 hPa) is now lower than C, so the wind there reverses and blows from C towards E. (e) As air flows in, the pressure at C rises until it equals the pressures around it, and then the flow stops, as the air flow between the two balloons stopped. The flow lasts only if the air at C keeps rising away, for example when heated ground warms the air at C so it rises and keeps the pressure low.
s: Part (a): all winds blow towards C, high to low pressure
Part (b): S and C, 9 hPa = 900 Pa
Part (c): E and C, only 1 hPa
Part (d): W-C wind stops; E-C wind reverses to blow from C to E
Part (e): inflow raises the pressure at C until it equals its surroundings; heated air rising at C keeps it low

questions.q: A storm with high-speed winds is expected in a coastal town. Which of these actions does NOT help to reduce damage from the wind?
questions.a: Shutting every door and window of a weak-roofed house tightly
o: Shutting every door and window of a weak-roofed house tightly
Opening doors and windows so the wind can pass through the house
Cutting large holes in the cloth of a big roadside hoarding
Fixing a weak roof more firmly to the walls before the storm

questions.q:
A weather map shows three nearby places: P at 1004 hPa, Q at 1010 hPa and R at 1004 hPa.
(a) Will wind blow between P and R? Why?
(b) In which direction will wind blow between Q and P?
questions.a: (a) No (no steady wind from this cause). Both are at the same pressure, and air moves only when there is a pressure difference. (b) From Q to P, from the higher pressure (1010 hPa) to the lower (1004 hPa).
s: Part (a): no wind, equal pressures
Part (b): from Q to P, high to low pressure

questions.q:
Before a storm, a shopkeeper cuts large holes in his cloth banner, and his neighbour opens the doors and windows of her house, which has a weak roof. Both say they are 'letting the wind through'.
(i) How do the holes protect the banner?
(ii) How do open doors and windows protect the roof? Name the two places whose pressures are being brought closer.
(iii) State one way in which the two ideas differ.
questions.a: (i) The holes let the wind pass through the banner, so less wind pushes on the cloth and the force on it and its ropes is reduced. (ii) When the wind moves through the house as well as over the roof, the pressure inside the house is lowered too, so the pressure difference between the inside of the house and the air above the roof becomes much smaller, and the roof is not lifted off. (iii) The banner is saved by reducing the direct push of the wind on it; the roof is saved by reducing a pressure difference between inside and above it caused by the fast wind lowering the pressure above it.
s: Part (i): wind passes through, so less force on the banner
Part (ii): inside the house and above the roof; their pressure difference is reduced
Part (iii): direct push reduced for the banner, pressure difference reduced for the roof

questions.q: Describe a situation from daily life (not balloons, cycle tubes or breezes) in which a difference in air pressure makes air move. Name the high-pressure region and the low-pressure region, and state when the air would stop moving.
questions.a: Example: opening the valve of a fully pumped football. Inside the ball the air pressure is high; outside it is lower. Air rushes out through the valve from inside (high) to outside (low), and stops when the pressure inside equals the pressure outside. (Any situation with a correct high and low region and the stopping condition earns the marks.)
s: A valid daily-life situation of air moving due to a pressure difference
High- and low-pressure regions correctly named
Air stops when the pressures become equal

questions.q:
On a hot afternoon, a large tarred parking lot heats up much faster than a shady grass park beside it.
(a) Over which of the two does a region of low pressure form? Explain.
(b) In which direction will a light breeze blow between them near the ground?
questions.a: (a) Over the parking lot. The air above the hotter lot becomes warmer and lighter and rises, leaving a region of low pressure. (b) From the park towards the parking lot, because air moves from the higher pressure over the cooler park to the lower pressure over the lot.
s: Part (a): over the hotter lot, where warm air rises
Part (b): from the park to the lot, high to low pressure

questions.q:
In a storm cloud, up-and-down winds rub ice particles and water droplets together; the ice particles become positively charged and the droplets negatively charged. Suppose that in some cloud the ice particles were the heavier ones and the droplets the lighter ones, with everything else the same.
(a) Which part of that cloud would then be positively charged? Explain.
(b) What charge would the ground below then take, and why?
questions.a: (a) The lower part. The lighter particles move to the upper part and the heavier ones stay in the lower part, so the heavier, positively charged ice particles would collect at the bottom and the negative droplets at the top. (b) Negative. In a real cloud the negatively charged lower part makes the ground below it positive, the opposite charge; by the same reasoning, a positively charged lower part would make the ground negative.
s: Part (a): lower part positive, because the heavier particles stay low
Part (b): negative, the ground takes the charge opposite to the cloud's lower part

questions.q:
A Kolkata school holds its sports day on a hot, humid April afternoon. At 4 p.m. a Kalboishakhi storm arrives with strong winds, rain, lightning and loud thunder, and the children are taken into the school buses. The school is also building a new block whose highest point, the top of a water tank, is 16 m above the ground. Three contractors quote for a lightning conductor.
Quote | Top of the pointed rod | Lower end of the rod | Price
A | 17 m above the ground | buried 3 m deep in the ground | Rs 18,000
B | 15 m above the ground | buried 3 m deep in the ground | Rs 12,000
C | 17 m above the ground | fixed to the wall at ground level | Rs 9,000
(a) Explain how the hot afternoon and the humid air together led to this storm.
(b) A child says the thunder is the sound of the clouds crashing into each other. What really produces it?
(c) What is wrong, if anything, with quotes B and C?
(d) The budget committee wants the cheapest quote. Which quote should the school accept? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The heated land made the warm, moist air rise, creating low pressure; cooler air flowed in, was heated and rose too, setting up strong winds. The rising air expanded and cooled, its moisture condensed into droplets and clouds, and the droplets merged into drops heavy enough to fall as rain. (b) Lightning rapidly heats the air around it; the air expands suddenly and produces the loud sound of thunder. (c) B: its pointed top (15 m) is below the highest point of the building (16 m); it must be higher. C: its lower end is not buried deep in the ground, so it gives the charges no easy path into the ground. (d) Quote A, though it costs the most. It is the only one whose top is above the highest point and whose lower end is buried deep, so only it can carry the charges safely into the ground; B and C are cheaper but would not protect the block.
s: Part (a): heated moist air rises, inflow and circulation; rising air cools and condenses into clouds and rain
Part (b): lightning heats the air, which expands suddenly
Part (c): B top below the highest point; C lower end not buried
Part (d): A, the only quote meeting both conditions, despite the cost

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: The ground below a storm cloud takes the charge opposite to the charge in the cloud's lower part.
Statement 2: Hail can fall from a storm even on a very hot day, because rising air can reach heights where the low temperature turns droplets into ice.
Statement 3: A flash that lights up only the inside of one cloud is not lightning, because lightning always passes between a cloud and the ground.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Storms are more frequent in Kerala than in a cold, dry region.
Reason (R): A storm forms when heated, moist air rises, cools and its moisture condenses into clouds and rain.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Two storm clouds build up the same kind of charge separation. In cloud X the build-up of charge stays moderate; in cloud Y it becomes very large. Which cloud is more likely to give a flash of lightning, and why?
questions.a: Y, as only a very large build-up breaks down air's insulation
o: Y, as only a very large build-up breaks down air's insulation
X, as a smaller charge passes through the air more easily
Both equally, as air lets charges flow through it at all times
Neither, as charges in the same cloud can never meet each other

questions.q: True or False? 'The ground and the trees below a storm cloud carry the same charge as the cloud's lower part, so lightning to the ground is simply that charge falling out of the cloud.' Give the verdict, then the correct explanation.
questions.a: False. The lower part of the cloud is negatively charged, and as it comes close to the ground it makes the ground and nearby objects such as trees positively charged, the opposite charge. Lightning is a sudden flow of charge when these opposite charges meet, once the build-up is so large that the insulating property of the air breaks down.
s: Verdict: False; the ground becomes positive, opposite to the negative cloud base
Lightning is the flow of charge when opposite charges meet as the air breaks down

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the explanation in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Hail falls from a storm on a very hot afternoon | a. The rod gives charges an easy path into the ground
2. A rumble follows a flash inside a cloud | b. Lightning heated the air, which expanded suddenly
3. The lower end of a lightning conductor is buried deep | c. Air insulates until the build-up of charge is very large
4. Charge builds up in a cloud for minutes before the first flash | d. Warm air rose so high that the droplets turned to ice

Weather data for three places on the same April afternoon:
Place | Ground temperature | Air
P | 40 C | very humid
Q | 41 C | very dry
R | 22 C | very humid
(a) Which place is most likely to have a storm this afternoon?
(b) Give the reason that rules out each of the other two.
questions.a: (a) P. (b) Q is hot, so warm air rises strongly, but its dry air holds little moisture to condense into clouds and rain. R has moist air, but its ground is not strongly heated, so warm, moist air does not rise strongly and set up the circulation of winds. A storm needs both heating and moisture, which only P has.
s: Part (a): P
Part (b): Q lacks moisture; R lacks strong heating to make the air rise

questions.q: A builder fits a lightning conductor to a new hospital block. Which one of these would stop it from protecting the building?
questions.a: Its lower end stops at the roof, not in the ground
o: Its lower end stops at the roof, not in the ground
Its top end is shaped into a sharp, narrow point
Its top end is higher than the highest point of the building
It is a metal rod running down along the outside wall

questions.q:
Thick rain clouds hang over a humid coastal town on a day when the air inside the clouds is almost still, with no strong winds blowing up and down.
(a) Would electric charges build up in these clouds? Explain.
(b) Could the rain from them be called a thunderstorm? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) No. Charges develop when strong winds blowing up and down rub ice particles and water droplets against each other; with still air there is no such rubbing, so no charge builds up. (b) No. Without a build-up of charge there is no lightning, and so no thunder; a thunderstorm is a storm with lightning and thunder.
s: Part (a): no, no up-and-down winds to rub particles and separate charge
Part (b): no, without charge there is no lightning or thunder

questions.q:
Mohan writes two definitions in his notebook:
(i) 'A storm is strong winds accompanied by rain.'
(ii) 'A thunderstorm is a storm in which the rain turns into hail.'
Is Mohan right, wrong, or partly right? Correct anything that is wrong.
questions.a: Partly right. (i) is correct: strong winds accompanied by rain make a storm. (ii) is wrong: a thunderstorm is a storm accompanied by lightning and thunder. Hail can fall from a storm, but it is not what makes a storm a thunderstorm.
s: Verdict: partly right
Definition (i) is correct
Definition (ii) corrected: a storm with lightning and thunder

questions.q: On a very hot afternoon in Jharkhand, a storm brings hailstones, small balls of ice, although the ground is hot. Explain in three steps how ice can fall from a storm on such a day.
questions.a: (1) The heated ground makes warm, moist air rise; as it rises it expands and cools, and its moisture condenses into water droplets, forming clouds. (2) Under certain conditions the warm air rises to such great heights that the low temperature there turns the water droplets into ice particles. (3) These ice particles, heavy enough to fall, come down to the ground as hail.
s: Rising warm, moist air cools and forms droplets and clouds
The air rises so high that the low temperature turns droplets into ice
The ice particles come down as hail

questions.q:
A village safety poster lists three tips for lightning:
(i) 'Shelter under a lone tall tree until the storm passes.'
(ii) 'If you are swimming in the pond, stay in the water until the rain stops.'
(iii) 'In an open area, find a low-lying spot and crouch down.'
Judge each tip and correct any that are wrong.
questions.a: (i) Wrong: during lightning we should stay away from tall objects, so do not shelter under a tall tree. (ii) Wrong: anyone in water should get out of it during lightning. (iii) Right: in an open area, find a low-lying spot and crouch down (keeping contact with the ground small, not lying flat).
s: Tip (i) wrong: stay away from tall objects
Tip (ii) wrong: get out of the water
Tip (iii) right: crouch in a low-lying open area

questions.q:
'Pre-monsoon thunderstorms in eastern India are both a blessing and a danger.' Justify this statement by answering the following.
(a) Name the local thunderstorms of West Bengal and of Assam.
(b) Give one way in which they are a blessing to farmers there, and say why their timing matters.
(c) Explain why such storms form so often in these regions in the hot months before the monsoon.
(d) Explain what must happen inside the storm clouds for lightning to occur.
(e) Name two kinds of harm the chapter says lightning can do, and explain why a person under a lone tall tree is in more danger than one crouching in a low-lying open area.
questions.a: (a) Kalboishakhi in West Bengal (also Bihar and Jharkhand) and Bordoisila in Assam. (b) They come before the arrival of the monsoon and help the kharif crops grow, giving rain at the time these crops need it. (c) These regions are hot and humid: strongly heated land makes warm, moist air rise; cooler air flows in and rises too, giving strong winds, and the rising air cools so that its moisture condenses into clouds and rain. Storms are more frequent in such hot, humid, tropical regions. (d) Strong winds blowing up and down rub ice particles and water droplets together, so charges develop and separate (positive above, negative below); when the build-up is very large, the insulating property of the air breaks down and charge flows as lightning. (e) Lightning can ignite fires, damage buildings and cause severe burns or death. The chapter tells us to stay away from tall objects during lightning, so standing under a tall tree is unsafe; crouching in a low-lying open area, with little contact with the ground, is the advised position.
s: Part (a): Kalboishakhi (West Bengal) and Bordoisila (Assam)
Part (b): before the monsoon, they help kharif crops grow
Part (c): heat makes moist air rise and circulate; it cools and condenses into clouds and rain
Part (d): up-and-down winds separate charge until the air breaks down
Part (e): fires, damage, burns or death; stay away from tall objects, crouch in a low open area

questions.q:
A teacher's chalkboard sketch of a thunderstorm shows a cloud with '-' (negative) written on its top part and '+' (positive) on its bottom part, and '-' written on the ground and trees below it.
(a) Which labels are wrong?
(b) What makes charges build up inside the cloud in the first place?
(c) Explain why the top and bottom of the cloud get the charges they really have.
(d) What charge do the ground and trees get, and why?
(e) What finally allows the charges to flow, producing lightning?
questions.a: (a) All three: the top of the cloud should be '+', the bottom '-', and the ground and trees '+'. (b) Strong winds blowing upwards and downwards rub water droplets and ice particles against each other, so static electric charges develop. (c) The lighter, positively charged ice particles move up to the top; the heavier, negatively charged water droplets occupy the lower part. (d) Positive: when the negatively charged lower part of the cloud comes close to the ground, it causes the ground and nearby objects such as trees and buildings to become positively charged. (e) Air normally acts as an insulator and keeps the opposite charges apart; when the build-up becomes very large, this insulating property breaks down and a sudden flow of charge produces lightning.
s: Part (a): all three labels are reversed
Part (b): up-and-down winds rub droplets and ice particles
Part (c): lighter positive ice rises, heavier negative droplets stay low
Part (d): ground and trees become positive due to the negative cloud base
Part (e): large build-up breaks down the insulating air

questions.q:
A weather observer near Jorhat, Assam, kept this log one April evening.
5:50 p.m. | Very hot and humid; tall dark clouds building up
6:10 p.m. | Strong, gusty winds; heavy rain begins
6:25 p.m. | A flash lights up the inside of one cloud; a rumble follows
6:40 p.m. | A flash from the cloud to the ground on a hill; loud thunder
7:30 p.m. | Wind and rain die down
Her note at the end says: 'The thunder at 6:40 caused the flash that I saw.'
(a) From what time could the event first be called a thunderstorm? Give the reason.
(b) What had to build up inside the cloud between 6:10 and 6:25 for the first flash to happen?
(c) Correct her final note.
(d) Two days later her log reads: 6:00 p.m. strong winds and heavy rain; 6:20 p.m. a flash between two clouds, then a rumble; 6:50 p.m. wind and rain stop. Her friend says it must be logged as a storm, not a thunderstorm, because no lightning reached the ground. Decide how it should be logged, and justify.
questions.a: (a) From 6:25 p.m. From 6:10 there were strong winds with rain (a storm), but it became a thunderstorm only when lightning and thunder came with it, at 6:25. (b) A very large separation of electric charge (positive above, negative below), built up by up-and-down winds rubbing ice particles and droplets, large enough to break down the insulating property of the air. (c) It is the other way round: the lightning flash heated the air around it, which expanded suddenly and produced the thunder. (d) As a thunderstorm. Lightning can occur within a cloud, between clouds or between a cloud and the ground, so the flash between two clouds was lightning, and the rumble was thunder. Strong winds with rain plus lightning and thunder make a thunderstorm; the lightning need not reach the ground.
s: Part (a): 6:25 p.m., when lightning and thunder joined the storm
Part (b): very large charge separation, enough to break down the air's insulation
Part (c): lightning caused the thunder by heating and expanding the air
Part (d): a thunderstorm, as lightning between clouds with thunder counts

questions.q: On a hot afternoon, a breeze blows into a town from the cooler fields around it. What happens to this cooler air once it reaches the heated town?
questions.a: It is heated and rises, so more air keeps flowing in
o: It is heated and rises, so more air keeps flowing in
It sinks and spreads back into the fields along the ground
It raises the pressure over the town, so the breeze ends
It cools at once and falls as rain over the nearby fields

questions.q:
In Kerala, a mango grower is happy when pre-monsoon thunderstorms arrive, but the same evening a football coach hurries his team off the open ground.
(a) Why does the grower welcome these storms?
(b) Why is the coach right to act quickly?
questions.a: (a) In Kerala these pre-monsoon thunderstorms, called mango showers, support the ripening of mangoes. (b) The storms bring lightning, which can cause severe burns or death; a player on an open ground is at risk, so the team must take shelter (a bus or car is comparatively safer).
s: Part (a): mango showers help mangoes ripen
Part (b): lightning can cause burns or death, so they must shelter

questions.q:
Suppose the warm, moist air rising over heated land did not cool at all as it rose.
(a) Would clouds form? Explain.
(b) Could a thunderstorm develop? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) No. Clouds form because the rising air expands and cools, so the moisture in it condenses into water droplets; without cooling there would be no condensation and no clouds. (b) No. With no clouds there would be no water droplets or ice particles to be rubbed together by the winds, so no charges, no lightning and no thunder.
s: Part (a): no cooling, no condensation, so no clouds
Part (b): no droplets or ice to charge, so no lightning or thunder

questions.q: Four people are caught out of doors in a thunderstorm. Who is the safest, going by the chapter?
questions.a: A boy sitting inside a closed car
o: A boy sitting inside a closed car
A girl crouching under a tall lone tree
A man lying flat on open, low ground
A woman under a metal-rod umbrella

questions.q: Two clouds hang over Patna. In cloud A the water droplets stay tiny and separate; in cloud B the droplets keep colliding and merging. From which cloud is rain more likely to fall soon, and why?
questions.a: Cloud B, as merged drops grow heavy enough to fall
o: Cloud B, as merged drops grow heavy enough to fall
Cloud A, as tiny drops fall faster than large drops
Neither, as rain can fall only after lightning
Cloud A, as separate drops carry no charge to hold them

questions.q: A weather map shows two cyclones. In cyclone X the pressure is 994 mb at the centre and 1008 mb at the outer edge; in cyclone Y it is 980 mb at the centre and 1008 mb at the outer edge, over the same distance. Which is likely to have the faster winds, and why?
questions.a: Y, as its pressure difference of 28 mb is twice X's
o: Y, as its pressure difference of 28 mb is twice X's
X, as its centre pressure of 994 mb is the higher
Both the same, as both outer edges read 1008 mb
X, as a smaller difference lets the air flow freely

questions.q:
In a growing cyclone, air from the surroundings keeps rushing in towards the low-pressure centre.
(a) Suppose this air simply piled up at the centre instead of rising. What would happen to the pressure there, and to the winds? Explain.
(b) What does the chapter say keeps the air at the centre rising, so that the pressure stays very low?
questions.a: (a) The pressure at the centre would rise until it equalled the pressure around it; with no pressure difference left, air would stop rushing in and the winds would die down. (b) As the moist air rises, its water vapour condenses into raindrops and releases heat; this warms the rising air further so it rises even more, creating an even lower pressure, and the inrushing air also starts rising.
s: Part (a): pressure at the centre rises until equal, so the winds die down
Part (b): heat released by condensation warms the air so it keeps rising

questions.q:
A district office on the Odisha coast tracks a cyclone on its weather screen.
Day | Where the cyclone is | Highest wind speed
1 | Far out over the warm Bay of Bengal | 110 km/h
2 | Over the sea, moving towards the coast | 170 km/h
3 | Over the sea, close to the coast | 220 km/h
4 | Has just crossed the coast | 160 km/h
5 | 300 km inland | 60 km/h
On Day 2, warnings say the cyclone will cross the coast near the fishing village of Pentha on Day 4.
(a) On which day was the cyclone strongest, and where was it? Explain why it kept strengthening until then.
(b) By what percentage did its highest wind speed fall from Day 4 to Day 5, and why did it weaken so much?
(c) Which danger from the sea is greatest for Pentha around Days 3 and 4, and what causes it?
(d) On Day 3 the sky over Pentha is still fairly clear, and some fishers want one last trip to sea, arguing that the cyclone has not yet reached land. Decide whether they should go, and justify using the table and your answers.
questions.a: (a) Day 3, over the sea close to the coast (220 km/h). Over the warm ocean it kept getting warm, moist air; the condensing vapour released heat, so the air rose further, the pressure dropped lower and the winds grew stronger. (b) (160 - 60) / 160 x 100 = 62.5 percent. Over land its source of moist air was cut off, so it gradually lost strength. (c) A storm surge: the cyclone's strong winds push ocean water towards the shore as a wall of water that can be 3 to 12 m high and flood the coast. (d) They should not go. Not having reached land does not make the sea safe: on Day 3 the cyclone is over the sea close to the coast at its strongest (220 km/h), and its winds are pushing the sea towards the shore. They should follow the IMD warnings and get ready to move to the shelter.
s: Part (a): Day 3, over the sea; warm moist air and heat from condensation strengthen it
Part (b): 62.5 percent; its moist-air supply is cut off over land
Part (c): storm surge, winds push sea water to the shore
Part (d): do not go; on Day 3 it is at its strongest over the sea near the coast

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: The eye of a cyclone has the strongest winds and the heaviest rain.
Statement 2: Fallen trees and debris blocking the roads after a cyclone can make it hard for help to reach the affected areas.
Statement 3: In a cyclone, winds blow outward from the centre towards the regions of higher pressure.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cyclone gradually loses strength after it reaches land.
Reason (R): The Earth's rotation causes the moving air in a cyclone to spin.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: True or False? 'A village 20 km from the sea can still be flooded when a cyclone strikes the coast.' Give the verdict, then two ways the chapter shows this can happen.
questions.a: True. The storm surge, a wall of seawater pushed ashore by the cyclone's winds, can flood not only coastal areas but even areas far from the sea; and the heavy rainfall that comes with a cyclone can make rivers overflow.
s: Verdict: True
Storm surge reaches areas far from the sea; heavy rain makes rivers overflow

questions.q:
Match each problem seen after a cyclone in Column I with its cause in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Wells in a coastal village turn salty | a. Long power outages
2. A hill road far inland is buried under mud and rocks | b. Fallen trees and debris on the roads
3. Relief trucks cannot reach a town for two days | c. Seawater rushing inland
4. A hospital has to run on generators for a week | d. Heavy rain setting off a landslide
Cyclones form over the warm waters of the Bay of Bengal but not over the hot sands of the Thar desert. Which reason fits the chapter?
questions.a: The warm sea supplies moist air whose condensing vapour releases heat
o: The warm sea supplies moist air whose condensing vapour releases heat
The sea turns with the Earth's rotation, but the desert sand does not
The desert has no differences in air pressure from place to place
A cyclone needs cold water to cool the air that rises above it

questions.q: Kiran says: 'The Earth's rotation plays no part in a cyclone. The spinning comes only from the warm air rising over the ocean.' Is Kiran right? Explain the part played by rising air and by the Earth's rotation.
questions.a: No. Warm, moist air rising over the ocean creates the very low pressure, and air from the surroundings rushes in and also rises. But the chapter says it is the Earth's rotation that causes this moving air to spin. Rising air alone gives the low pressure and the inflow; the rotation gives the spin that makes it a spinning system, a cyclone.
s: Verdict: Kiran is wrong
Rising warm air creates low pressure and the inflow of air
The Earth's rotation makes the moving air spin

questions.q:
A cyclone is moving steadily across a coastal town. After hours of fierce wind and rain, the wind suddenly drops and the rain stops. Some people step outside, thinking the cyclone is over.
(a) Which part of the cyclone is most likely over the town now?
(b) Why is it unsafe to go out?
questions.a: (a) The eye, the calm region of lowest pressure at the centre. (b) The eye is surrounded by the region of strong winds and heavy rain. As the cyclone keeps moving, the other side of that region will pass over the town, bringing the violent winds and rain back.
s: Part (a): the eye of the cyclone
Part (b): the eye is ringed by strong winds and rain, which will return as the cyclone moves on

questions.q:
A weather map shows a cyclone as rings of equal pressure. Going inward, the rings read 1008 mb, 998 mb, 996 mb and 994 mb at the centre.
(a) Where is the eye of this cyclone, and how do you know?
(b) In which direction does the air near the surface move: towards the centre or away from it? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) At the centre, inside the 994 mb ring, because the eye is the region of lowest pressure. (b) Towards the centre, because air moves from regions of higher pressure (1008 mb outside) to lower pressure (994 mb at the centre).
s: Part (a): at the 994 mb centre, the lowest pressure
Part (b): inward, from high to low pressure

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a sensible step for families in a cyclone-prone coastal district?
questions.a: Making no plans 20 km inland, as cyclones weaken on land
o: Making no plans 20 km inland, as cyclones weaken on land
Keeping an emergency kit of essential items ready at home
Following the alerts and warnings issued by the IMD
Moving quickly to the nearby designated cyclone shelter

questions.q:
The Amphan cyclone in 2020 had peak wind speeds of 270 km/h. A strong local thunderstorm in the same region brought gusts of 90 km/h.
(a) How many times faster were Amphan's peak winds than the thunderstorm's gusts?
(b) Give two other destructive effects of a cyclone that the chapter describes, and say what in the cyclone causes each.
questions.a: (a) 270 / 90 = 3 times faster. (b) Any two, each with its cause: a storm surge flooding coastal areas and even areas far from the sea, caused by strong winds pushing ocean water towards the shore; rivers overflowing and landslides, caused by the heavy rainfall; drinking water and farmland spoiled, caused by seawater rushing inland (its salt makes soil less fertile); roads blocked, caused by fallen trees and debris; power outages lasting days.
s: Part (a): 3 times
First effect with its cause

questions.q:
Six cards describe how a cyclone forms, but they are jumbled, and ONE card contains a mistake.
P: Air from the surrounding regions rushes in and sinks down to the sea.
Q: The ocean water gets heated and the warm, moist air above it rises.
R: The Earth's rotation makes the moving air spin.
S: The water vapour condenses into raindrops, releasing heat.
T: The rising air is warmed further, rises even more, and the pressure drops even lower.
U: A very low-pressure area forms with high-speed winds revolving around it.
(a) Which card has the mistake? Write it correctly.
(b) Arrange the corrected cards in order.
(c) Explain why card T leads to card P.
(d) Suppose the Earth stopped rotating. Which card would no longer happen, and would a cyclone still form? Explain what would form instead.
questions.a: (a) Card P. The inrushing air does not sink; it also starts rising. Correct card: 'Air from the surrounding regions rushes in and also starts rising.' (b) Q, S, T, P, R, U. (c) As the air rises more, the pressure at the centre drops even lower, and air from the surrounding higher-pressure regions rushes in towards this low pressure. (d) Card R. Warm, moist air would still rise and make a low-pressure area, and air would still rush in and rise, but nothing would make the moving air spin. So there would be no spinning system of clouds, winds and rain, that is, no cyclone, only rising air with air flowing in to a low-pressure area.
s: Part (a): card P; the inrushing air also rises
Part (b): order Q, S, T, P, R, U
Part (c): lower pressure draws in air from higher-pressure surroundings
Part (d): card R would not happen; low pressure and inflow remain but no spin, so no cyclone

questions.q:
A school 1 km from the beach in coastal Odisha is writing its cyclone plan.
(a) Where should the school get its information about an approaching cyclone, and what do weather satellites now make possible?
(b) Why should students and staff move to the shelter as soon as a warning comes, instead of waiting for the wind to rise?
(c) Why must an emergency kit be ready before the cyclone, rather than bought after it?
(d) The school's land is 3 m above sea level. Use the chapter's figure for the height of a storm surge to judge whether the school could be flooded, and say what this means for the plan.
(e) A parent expects school to reopen the day after the cyclone passes. Why might it take much longer?
questions.a: (a) From weather reports and the alerts and warnings issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD); satellites let us track a cyclone and predict its path in advance. (b) Fallen trees and debris can block roads and make it hard for people to move or for help to reach them, so moving early is safer. (c) Power outages can last for days and disrupt emergency services and daily life, so essential items must already be at hand. (d) Yes, it could be flooded. The chapter says the surge pushed ashore by a cyclone can be a wall of water 3 to 12 m high, which is as high as or higher than the school's 3 m land, and it can flood coastal areas. So the plan must be to move everyone early to the designated cyclone shelter, not to stay in the school. (e) A cyclone leaves a trail of destruction that can take months or even years to repair: blocked roads, power cuts and spoiled water supplies all take time to fix.
s: Part (a): IMD alerts and warnings; satellites track and predict the path
Part (b): roads may get blocked by fallen trees and debris
Part (c): power outages last days and disrupt services
Part (d): yes, a 3 to 12 m surge can reach 3 m land, so move to the designated shelter
Part (e): damage can take months or years to repair

questions.q:
Before a cyclone strikes, officials forecast a storm surge up to 8 m high. Two villages are in its path.
Village | Height of land above sea level | Distance from the sea
B | 15 m | 0.5 km
C | 6 m | 8 km
There are buses enough to move only one village's people before the cyclone arrives.
(a) What is a storm surge, and what causes it?
(b) One official says village C is safe because it is 8 km from the sea. Use the chapter to show why distance alone does not make it safe.
(c) Another official wants the buses sent to village B because it is only 0.5 km from the sea. Which village should get the buses? Justify using the data.
(d) After the cyclone, C's fields and wells stayed under seawater for two days. Give two problems this leaves behind, with reasons.
questions.a: (a) Strong winds during a cyclone push ocean water towards the shore, creating a wall of water, 3 to 12 m high, called a storm surge. (b) The chapter says the surge can flood coastal areas and even areas far from the sea, so being 8 km away does not by itself keep C dry. (c) Village C. Its land (6 m) is lower than the 8 m surge, so the wall of water can flood it. B is close to the sea, but its land (15 m) is higher than the surge, so the surge cannot cover it. (d) The well water is unsafe to drink, because seawater rushing inland contaminates drinking water sources; the next crop may be poor, because the salt in seawater makes the soil less fertile.
s: Part (a): winds push seawater ashore as a wall of water
Part (b): the surge can reach areas far from the sea
Part (c): village C, land below the 8 m surge; B is above it
Part (d): wells contaminated; salt makes the soil less fertile

questions.q:
Satellites first spot a cyclone when it is 900 km from the coast. It moves straight towards the coast at a steady 15 km/h.
(a) How many hours of warning does this give before it reaches the coast?
(b) Twelve hours later, how far from the coast is it, and what is it that lets weather offices give such early warnings?
questions.a: (a) 900 / 15 = 60 hours. (b) In 12 hours it moves 12 x 15 = 180 km, so it is 900 - 180 = 720 km from the coast. Weather monitoring satellites let us track cyclones and predict their path, so the IMD can issue alerts and warnings early.
s: Part (a): 60 hours
Part (b): 720 km; satellites track the cyclone and predict its path

questions.q: Show that the eye of a cyclone cannot be a region of high pressure, using how a cyclone forms and how air moves.
questions.a: (1) A cyclone forms as warm, moist air keeps rising over the ocean, so the pressure at the centre keeps dropping; its centre is the very low-pressure area. (2) Air from the surroundings rushes in towards the centre, and air moves only from higher to lower pressure. (3) If the eye were a region of high pressure, air would move outward from it, not rush in; so the eye must be the region of lowest pressure.
s: Rising air keeps lowering the pressure at the centre
Air rushes in, and air moves from high to low pressure
A high-pressure eye would push air outward, a contradiction
